extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, biomedical researchers, and research-policy makers interested in data-sharing, reproducibility, and preprint-to-publication practices
extracted.subtask_description: Classifying and assessing the sufficiency/openness of data availability statements (DAS) in medRxiv preprints and their published counterparts, and evaluating journal data-sharing policies' effect on DAS openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 0 — Not applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not applicable (protocol for a review, commentary, etc)" — statements indicating no datasets were generated or analysed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Data sharing not applicable to this article as no datasets were generated or analysed during the current study." Records categorized as 'Not applicable' at either the preprint or published stage were excluded from further analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 1 — Data not made available (Closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit statement that data are not made available to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Not available for public". Treated as 'closed' data in the classification system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 2 — Data available on request to authors (Closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement that data can be obtained by contacting the authors / on reasonable request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Data can be available upon reasonable request to the corresponding author." The paper notes this is a common anti-pattern: prior work shows many 'available on request' claims are not upheld, especially over time. Such statements count as 'closed' and represent insufficient openness unless backed by verifiable access mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 3 — Data will be made available on publication (link provided) (Closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors state data will be deposited/available in the future and provide a link to an embargoed repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "The protocol and full dataset will be available at Open Science Framework upon peer review publication (https://osf.io/rvbuy/)." Used for preprints but not used when categorizing published articles (see rule for published-stage categorization). Analysis tracked whether these promises were fulfilled on publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 4 — Data will be made available on publication (no link provided) (Closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors say data will be deposited/made available in future but give no link or repository details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Data will be deposited in Dryad upon publication" (no accession/link). Considered 'closed' at preprint stage; evaluated on whether promise was fulfilled on publication. For published-stage categorization Categories 3 and 4 are not used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 5 — Data available from central repository but insufficient detail to locate dataset (Closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data drawn from a central repository (access-controlled or not) but the DAS lacks sufficient detail to identify the specific dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Data were obtained from the international MSBase cohort study. Information regarding data availability can be obtained at https://www.msbase.org/." This is considered 'closed' because readers cannot uniquely find the study-specific dataset from the statement alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 6 — Data available from central access-controlled repository with sufficient identifiers (Closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data held in an access-controlled central repository but the statement provides sufficient details (application number, accession ID, date stamps) to identify the dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "This research has been conducted using the UK Biobank Resource under application number 24494. All bona fide researchers can apply to use the UK Biobank resource..." Treated as 'closed' (access-controlled) but with enough metadata for findability/identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 7 — Data available in manuscript or supporting file (Open)
rubrics_metrics.description: All data related to the study are present within the paper or supplementary files (e.g., S1 File).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "All data related to this study are present in the paper or the S1 File." For large samples the authors took such claims at face value (did not verify content), which they note may overestimate true availability — prior work suggests linked data may still be incomplete or missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 8 — Data available via online repository not access-controlled (Open)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data deposited in an online repository that is not access-controlled (e.g., Dryad, Zenodo) and is directly accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "Extracted data used in this meta-analysis and analysis code are available at www.doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3149365." Considered 'open' because data can be obtained without restrictions; this is the clearest form of openness in the classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open versus Closed data definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary distinction: whether data used in the study are openly available without restriction ('open') or not ('closed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The classification system grouped categories into 'open' (e.g., data in manuscript or open repository) and 'closed' (not available, available on request, embargoed, access-controlled). The authors based the system on the 'Findability' and 'Accessibility' elements of the FAIR framework and previous categorizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use FAIR principles for classification (Findability & Accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification built on the FAIR guiding principles' 'Findability' and 'Accessibility' elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scheme draws on prior studies and FAIR to judge whether a DAS provides sufficient information (e.g., links, accession IDs) to find and access datasets. Emphasis on providing repository links/identifiers to make data findable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative categorization rule: most restrictive aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a DAS mentions multiple data sources with varying openness, classify the statement according to its most restrictive component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a statement lists some data in the manuscript but other parts only 'available on request', the DAS is classified as the more restrictive category (closed). This conservative approach avoids overstating openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published-stage categorization exclusion of future-availability categories
rubrics_metrics.description: When categorizing published articles' DAS, do not use categories indicating 'data available in future' (Categories 3 and 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the published stage should have resolved future-availability promises, Categories 3 and 4 (data will be available in the future) are not applied to published article DAS; published DAS are categorized using the remaining groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinded, independent dual coding with consensus resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: DAS coding should be performed by at least two independent reviewers blinded to preprint metadata, with disagreements resolved through discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study, two independent researchers classified statements while blind to title/author/institution to avoid bias; disagreements were resolved by discussion. This produced high inter-rater reliability (Cohen's Kappa = 0.98). This is a recommended reliability method for DAS evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude 'Not applicable' records from openness analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Records whose DAS are 'Not applicable' (e.g., no datasets generated) should be removed from analyses of openness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study 4.0% of preprints were Category 0 and excluded from further analyses. This prevents conflating non-data articles with data-sharing behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal policy binary classification (mandates vs does not mandate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify journal data-sharing policies as either mandating/ requiring data sharing (1) or not (0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where journals had no obvious policy they were classified as not mandating. Note that 'not mandating' can include journals that merely encourage data sharing. Use this binary to stratify changes in DAS openness between preprint and published stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome metric: change in openness between stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a record becomes 'more open', 'more closed', or shows 'no change' when moving from preprint to published DAS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'more open' as change from any 'closed' category at preprint stage to an 'open' category at publication; 'more closed' is the reverse. Use categorical assignments to compute counts/proportions and stratify by journal policy (mandate vs not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of promises to make data available on publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow up preprints that promise future availability (Categories 3 and 4) to see whether data were actually made available in the published article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare whether including a link to an embargoed repository at preprint influences realization on publication. In the study only a small proportion of such promises were observed to be fulfilled; track outcomes per preprint-to-publication pair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code availability capture and assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether programming code availability is described in the full-text manuscript and whether DAS capture that information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a random sample of 400 preprints, code availability in the full text was coded as 'code availability described' vs 'code availability not described', and compared to whether the DAS mentioned code. The study found many instances where code was described in the manuscript but not recorded in the DAS, indicating DAS alone are insufficient to capture code sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity limitation / do not assume DAS claims equal true access
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that coding DAS categories does not verify that linked data are actually accessible; DAS claims may be untrue or incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors did not verify that data categorized as 'available in manuscript' or 'in repository' were actually retrievable; previous work indicates such veracity problems are common. Consequently, results based on DAS alone may overestimate true availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial enforcement requirement for effective data sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring a DAS is necessary but not sufficient; journals should enforce strict data-sharing policies and review DAS content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation based on findings: journals that mandate data sharing as a condition of publication showed larger increases in openness from preprint to publication. Enforcement and editorial/peer review of DAS contents (not just requiring the field) are important to make data actually available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce dedicated code availability statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a separate, standardized code availability statement in manuscripts to capture analytic code sharing explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because DAS often fail to capture code availability, journals should add a code availability section (or composite 'materials' availability) and critically assess it as part of editorial and peer review to aid reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign a data/code-focused reviewer or editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign an editor or reviewer whose sole responsibility is to examine the data and code provided with submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specialist would judge the adequacy of provided materials and evaluate authors' justifications for not sharing. The study cites prior proposals that this approach could address feasibility limits of expecting all reviewers to assess data/code.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLOS data policy standard (example of strong requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS requires authors to make all data underlying findings fully available without restriction, with rare exceptions; data should be part of the manuscript/supporting information or deposited in a public repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy expects underlying data points (not just summary statistics) to be available; if sharing is restricted (e.g., participant privacy), restrictions must be specified. This is an exemplar of a strict journal-level requirement used as a benchmark in the study.
